questions.question: Does the repository have a game-level dataset large enough to test a strategy?
questions.known: Yes. 7,239 regular-season games 1999-2026; 7,103 have final scores; 5,228 carry an observed price on both sides of the spread.
questions.answer: Yes, but only seasons from 2006 onward can be scored as bets, because earlier seasons carry a closing line with no price.
questions.blocks: Without a price, a bet cannot be scored honestly; assuming -110 would manufacture a result.

questions.question: Is the dataset's sign convention for the spread proven or assumed?
questions.known: Proven from the data: the closing spread correlates +0.431 with the actual home margin over 6,975 games (95% CI 0.412 to 0.450), so a positive number is the points the HOME team is favoured by.
questions.answer: Positive spread = home favourite. No assumption is needed.
questions.blocks: An inverted convention silently flips every bet result.

questions.question: Are our own lines more accurate than the market closing line?
questions.known: No. Spread MAE 10.70 points versus the market's 10.24 over 6,975 games; the market line is closer to the result in a paired test with t = 10.33.
questions.answer: No. The market line is more accurate than our line on this sample.
questions.blocks: Any strategy that simply replaces the market line with ours will lose the vig.

questions.question: Does our line add information the market line does not already contain?
questions.known: Yes, statistically. Regressing the actual margin on both lines gives a market weight of 0.953 and a model weight of 0.161 (standard error 0.048, t = 3.35, n = 6,975).
questions.unknown: How much of that increment survives real prices and real juice is not yet measured.
questions.answer: Yes: our disagreement with the closing line carries information at t = 3.35, even though our line is the less accurate of the two.
questions.discover: Blend the two lines and score the blend at observed prices; that is the next experiment.

questions.question: Can the raw edge correlation be called real?
questions.known: The correlation between (our line minus market line) and (result minus market line) is 0.019 (95% CI -0.005 to 0.042, p = 0.113).
questions.unknown: Whether the true value is small-positive or zero.
questions.blocks: The headline incremental test and the raw edge correlation disagree in significance; both are published and neither is hidden.
questions.discover: More seasons, and a blend experiment that converts the increment into a priced bet.

questions.question: Does any of the twelve published strategies beat the closing line at its real price?
questions.known: No strategy passes all eight gates. Best on return: S07 fade the road favourite of 7+, 401 bets, 55.6% hit rate against a 52.3% break-even, +6.06% ROI, p = 0.199, six of eight gates.
questions.answer: No. Nothing passes; one strategy is close enough to watch.
questions.blocks: Any claim of a winning system from this sample would be a claim luck can explain.

questions.question: Is there a signal that is reliably WRONG, and therefore useful in reverse?
questions.known: Yes. S09, backing the under when the closing total is 40 or lower, returned -7.93% over 887 bets with a 47.1% hit rate against a 51.3% break-even (p = 0.015, BH-adjusted 0.178).
questions.unknown: Whether the effect is a real pricing bias or a sample artefact; it does not survive multiple testing across twelve rules.
questions.answer: Suggestive but not proven: low closing totals have been priced too low in this sample.
questions.discover: Re-test the same rule on a future season before acting on it; do not trade it on this evidence.

questions.question: How much of each result could be luck?
questions.known: Under the null that the observed prices are fair, a one-unit bet at decimal d has variance d-1, so the standard deviation of total profit is the square root of the sum of (d-1) over the bets actually placed. For S07 that is 19.0 units against a realised 24.3.
questions.answer: For every strategy except S09 the realised profit sits inside the 95% band a lucky run would produce.
questions.blocks: Publishing a winner from inside that band would be publishing luck.

questions.question: How many bets would a strategy need before its edge could be detected?
questions.known: At the observed effect sizes: S07 about 1,950 bets, S04 about 11,872, S03 about 21,856, S05 about 314,129.
questions.answer: Far more than a season contains for every candidate except S07, and even S07 needs roughly twelve more seasons of 401 bets.
questions.blocks: Sample size, not model quality, is the binding constraint here.

questions.question: Are parlay legs in different games independent?
questions.known: Across 66 priced two-leg combinations, the ratio of the realised joint hit rate to the product of the two legs' own hit rates averages 1.0002 (median 0.998).
questions.answer: Yes, to within noise: the product rule is a fair price for parlays built from different games.

questions.question: Are parlay legs inside the SAME game independent?
questions.known: No. A quarterback's passing yards and his top receiver's receiving yards correlate +0.672 (95% CI 0.655 to 0.689, n = 3,989). The top two receivers on one team correlate +0.495. A team's passing and rushing yards correlate -0.239.
questions.answer: No, strongly not. Same-game combinations are worth materially more or less than the product of their legs.
questions.blocks: Any same-game parlay priced at the product of its legs is mispriced by assumption.
questions.discover: Prices for same-game parlays are not published in any official source, so the size of the mispricing cannot be measured here.

questions.question: Is the favourite covering correlated with the game going over?
questions.known: The phi correlation is 0.009 (95% CI -0.014 to 0.033, p = 0.444, n = 6,975).
questions.answer: No detectable correlation in this sample.

questions.question: Does a team's scoring persist from one week to the next?
questions.known: The lag-1 autocorrelation of a team's points scored is 0.141 (95% CI 0.125 to 0.158, n = 13,313 team-week pairs).
questions.answer: Slightly, and statistically real, but far too small to bet on after juice.
questions.blocks: 'Hot offence' systems are betting on a 0.14 correlation.

questions.question: Does weather move the total?
questions.known: Wind speed correlates -0.092 with total points (95% CI -0.120 to -0.065, p < 0.001, n = 4,931). Temperature correlates +0.009 (p = 0.517).
questions.answer: Wind does, a little, and in the expected direction. Temperature does not.
questions.discover: Weather is only recorded for 4,931 of 7,103 played games, so any weather rule is already restricted to that subset.

questions.question: Can injuries be tracked from an official source for the current week?
questions.known: Yes. The official nfl.com injury report for week 10 of 2026 is published at nfl.com/injuries/ and was read directly during this session.
questions.answer: Yes, but game designations are posted late: only the Thursday and early-Sunday clubs had final statuses at fetch time.

questions.question: Does the mirrored feed we use for history match the official page on game designations?
questions.known: No. For week 10 of 2026 the mirror holds 276 rows across 26 clubs, of which only 6 carry a game designation, while the official page shows designations for the clubs whose games are within 48 hours.
questions.blocks: Historical injury rules must be built on practice status, not game status, or they silently lose most of the signal.
questions.discover: Re-fetch the official page each day and record when each club's designation appears.

questions.question: Does the injury report alone produce a bettable edge?
questions.known: Two rules were tested on 2016-2026. Fading the club whose quarterback is ruled Out or Doubtful: 380 bets, -1.51% ROI. Fading the club with three or more more Out players: 685 bets, -0.30% ROI.
questions.answer: No. Both are indistinguishable from zero after juice.
questions.discover: A depth-chart-aware version (how good the replacement is) is the obvious next test, but historical depth charts are only available for 2026.

questions.question: Can second, third and fourth string replacements be tracked?
questions.known: Weekly depth charts with a position rank (1 = listed starter) exist for the current season and are joined to the injury report by session 7600ed8b in data/model/availability.json.
questions.unknown: Historical depth charts for earlier seasons are not in this repository, so a backup-quality rule cannot be back-tested yet.
questions.blocks: The single most-requested feature -- 'is the backup any good?' -- cannot be validated without historical depth charts.
questions.discover: Add the historical depth_charts releases to the collector and re-run; the join code already exists.

questions.question: Are there official or book-level prices for player props?
questions.known: No. Nothing in this repository's sources carries a prop price, and the NFL does not publish one.
questions.blocks: No prop bet can be scored, so no prop profit is claimed anywhere on this site.
questions.discover: A licensed price feed would be required; that is a purchasing decision, not an analysis one.

questions.question: Are the prices used for game bets real or assumed?
questions.known: Real. Every one of the 14,440 scored bets carries a price taken from the source file. Games with no price (1,902 of 7,103 played) train the ratings but are never scored.
questions.answer: Real, and the coverage is published season by season on the verification page.

questions.question: Do the computed standings match the official table?
questions.known: 32 of 32 clubs match on wins, losses, ties, points for and points against after recomputing every 2026 result from the game log.

questions.question: Do the game results match an independent transcription?
questions.known: 136 of 136 2026 results match the hand transcription in data/verified/games_2026.csv, after applying the published AZ/ARI club-code alias.

questions.question: Is there more than one site generation in the repository?
questions.known: Yes: a root generation (index.html plus pages/), a second under docs/, a third under verified-lab/, and an audit tree under referee/. They were built by different sessions and were deliberately preserved rather than overwritten.
questions.answer: Yes, four, and this session adds a fifth instead of deleting any of them.
questions.blocks: A reader cannot tell which numbers are current.
questions.discover: A single consolidation pass, taken as a decision rather than by one session acting alone.

questions.question: Can the leaderboard pay real rewards?
questions.known: The prior sessions flagged that rewards with monetary value need legal review, and the leaderboard published there is paper points only.
questions.unknown: Whether any reward structure is lawful in the relevant jurisdiction.
questions.blocks: Publishing a reward schedule before legal review.
questions.discover: Legal review, then a written rules document; the scoring model on the leaderboard page can then be reused unchanged.

suggestions.title: Blend our line with the market line and score the blend
suggestions.problem: Our line is less accurate than the closing line (MAE 10.70 vs 10.24) but adds statistically significant information to it (weight 0.161, t = 3.35). Neither fact alone tells you what to do.

options.name: A. Ship the raw model line as the house line
options.risk: High: it is measurably worse than the market and will lose the vig.

options.name: B. Publish a market-first blend, weight chosen out of sample
options.risk: Medium: the blend weight must be selected on earlier seasons only, or it is fitted to the answer.

options.name: C. Publish both lines side by side and let the reader choose
options.risk: Low, but it hands the decision back to the user with no guidance.

suggestions.recommendation: B, with the weight selected by nested walk-forward selection exactly as the half-life already is.

suggestions.title: Add historical depth charts so backup quality can be back-tested
suggestions.problem: The most-requested feature is knowing whether the second or third string replacement is any good. The current season's depth charts are joined to the injury report, but history is missing, so no backup-quality rule can be validated.

options.name: A. Add the historical depth_charts releases to the collector
options.risk: Low; the join code already exists and the files are large but pinnable by sha256.

options.name: B. Proxy backup quality with years of experience and prior snap share
options.risk: Medium; a proxy is not the thing being measured and must be labelled as a proxy.

options.name: C. Leave it and report only listed starters out
options.risk: Low accuracy, no false precision.

suggestions.recommendation: A. It is the only option that measures the thing the brief asks for.

suggestions.title: Log the official injury page daily and record when each club posts its game designation
suggestions.problem: The mirrored feed lags the official page on game designations: 6 of 276 week-10 rows carry one. A rule built on game status would silently lose most of its input.

options.name: A. Scrape the official page several times a day and store snapshots
options.risk: Low; the scraper already exists in pipeline/scrape_injuries.py.

options.name: B. Use practice status only and drop game status
options.risk: Medium; it throws away the single strongest availability signal.

options.name: C. Accept the lag and label every injury rule as practice-only
options.risk: Honest but strictly weaker.

suggestions.recommendation: A, with the snapshot time stored on every row so a reader knows exactly how stale a designation is.

suggestions.title: Collapse four site generations into one, as a decision rather than by one session acting alone
suggestions.problem: There are four preserved site generations (root, docs/, verified-lab/, referee/) plus this one. A reader cannot tell which numbers are current.

options.name: A. Keep all generations and add a prominent 'which numbers are current' banner
options.risk: Low, but the confusion stays.

options.name: B. Nominate one generation as current and demote the rest to an archive index
options.risk: Medium; it edits other sessions' pages, so it needs to be logged as a cross-session request.

options.name: C. Delete the older generations
options.risk: High; it destroys merged work that the coordination rules exist to protect.

suggestions.recommendation: A now, B logged as a cross-session request for the next integration session.

suggestions.title: Re-test the low-total under rule out of sample before anyone acts on it
suggestions.problem: Backing the under when the closing total is 40 or lower lost 7.93% over 887 bets (p = 0.015, BH-adjusted 0.178). That is the strongest single result in the study and it is a loss. It is exactly the kind of result that is a real bias and exactly the kind that is a sample artefact.

options.name: A. Pre-register the rule and score it on the next season before using it
options.risk: Low; this is the correct scientific response.

options.name: B. Trade the reverse of it now
options.risk: High; it does not survive multiple testing across twelve rules.

options.name: C. Ignore it
options.risk: Medium; it may be throwing away the only real finding.

suggestions.recommendation: A. Pre-registration is cheap and it is the difference between a finding and a story.

suggestions.title: Buy or build a price feed for player props, or stop listing props as a track
suggestions.problem: The leaderboard offers a player-prop track, but no prop price exists in any source this repository can reach, so no prop entry can ever be scored.

options.name: A. Obtain a licensed prop price feed
options.risk: Medium; cost and licensing.

options.name: B. Keep the prop track for projections and calibration only, with prices left blank
options.risk: Low; this is what the site does today.

options.name: C. Remove the prop track entirely
options.risk: Loses the projection and correlation work, which is real.

suggestions.recommendation: B now, A only if the projections prove skilful enough to be worth pricing.

suggestions.title: Improve the player projections before pricing them
suggestions.problem: Against a league-mean baseline the walk-forward projections remove 13.6% of the error for running-back rushing yards, 4.8% for receptions, 0.2% for quarterback passing yards and 0.06% for receiver receiving yards. Two of the four markets are barely better than guessing the league average.

options.name: A. Add team pass rate, game total and the opponent's rate as features
options.risk: Low; all three are knowable before kick-off.

options.name: B. Fit a proper distribution, not a point projection, so over/under prices can be implied
options.risk: Low; needed anyway if prices ever arrive.

options.name: C. Publish the current projections with their honest skill numbers
options.risk: Low; this is what the site does today.

suggestions.recommendation: C immediately, then A, then B. Do not price a projection that beats the league mean by 0.2%.

suggestions.title: Report the same-game parlay correlations on the bet slip itself
suggestions.problem: A quarterback's passing yards and his top receiver's receiving yards correlate +0.672. A parlay priced at the product of its legs ignores that entirely.

options.name: A. Show the measured correlation next to every same-game combination
options.risk: Low; the numbers are already computed.

options.name: B. Refuse to price same-game combinations
options.risk: Low but unhelpful.

options.name: C. Price them at the product and say nothing
options.risk: High; it is the standard industry failure mode.

suggestions.recommendation: A. It costs nothing and it is the difference between an informed combination and a guess.

suggestions.title: Publish the sample size a strategy needs, next to its return
suggestions.problem: Every strategy page shows a return. Returns on 400 bets are mostly noise, and the reader has no way to see that.

options.name: A. Show the 95% luck band and the bets-needed number beside every return
options.risk: Low; both are already computed.

options.name: B. Hide any strategy below 200 bets
options.risk: Medium; it hides information rather than explaining it.

options.name: C. Leave the leaderboard as a ranked table
options.risk: High; a ranked table of noise invites exactly the wrong conclusion.

suggestions.recommendation: A, and this site already does it on the leaderboard page.

suggestions.title: Automate the refresh so the board is never stale
suggestions.problem: The research extract and every model output are generated by scripts. If nobody runs them, the site silently shows last week's numbers.

options.name: A. Keep the existing daily Actions schedule
options.risk: Low.

options.name: B. Add a build-fails-loudly step that opens an issue when the refresh fails
options.risk: Low and worth doing.

options.name: C. Run it manually
options.risk: High; manual steps get skipped.

suggestions.recommendation: A plus B. A silent stale dashboard is worse than a broken one.

suggestions.title: Add a decision log that records who chose which path and when
suggestions.problem: The suggestions page offers paths, but once a path is chosen there is nowhere to record the decision, the evidence behind it, or who made it.
suggestions.evidence: Brief requirement: 'a section dedicated for suggestions so someone can review suggestions and choose the best path'

options.name: A. A decision-record table with status, chosen option, decider and date
options.risk: Low.

options.name: B. Free-text notes
options.risk: Medium; unsearchable and unversioned.

options.name: C. Nothing
options.risk: High; the review step has no memory.

suggestions.recommendation: A, and this site ships one with every suggestion set to 'awaiting decision'.

suggestions.title: Separate 'unverified' from 'verified blank' in every table
suggestions.problem: A blank cell can mean the value does not exist or that nobody has checked. Those are different and the reader cannot tell them apart.

options.name: A. A status column per row: verified, unverified, or not published by the source
options.risk: Low.

options.name: B. Colour the blanks
options.risk: Medium; inaccessible to colour-blind readers and lost in print.

options.name: C. Leave blanks blank
options.risk: Medium; ambiguous.

suggestions.title: Extend the sample backwards with official results, not another mirror
suggestions.problem: Only 5,228 of 7,103 played games carry a price, and prices start in 2006. Every significance test is limited by that.

options.name: A. Transcribe pre-2006 prices from an archive
options.risk: Medium; transcription errors are a real hazard.

options.name: B. Accept 2006 onward and publish the limit
options.risk: Low; this is what the site does.

options.name: C. Model the missing prices
options.risk: High; a modelled price is an assumed price, which is exactly what this project refuses to do.

suggestions.recommendation: B. Option C in particular would undo the whole premise of the build.

suggestions.title: Record the referee, roof and surface assignments for every game and test them
suggestions.problem: The extract carries referee, roof, surface, temperature and wind. Only weather has been tested so far (wind r = -0.092 with total points).

options.name: A. Test referee totals and sides tendencies with the same eight gates
options.risk: Low; the columns already exist.

options.name: B. Test dome versus outdoor
options.risk: Low.

options.name: C. Leave them untested
options.risk: Low, but it leaves cheap information on the table.

suggestions.recommendation: A and B, but only with the same multiple-testing correction applied to every other rule.

flags.item: Prop prices do not exist in any reachable official source
flags.detail: No player-prop entry can be scored, so the prop track publishes projections, calibration and correlations only. No prop profit is claimed anywhere.
flags.impact: The player-prop leaderboard track cannot rank anyone until a price feed exists.

flags.item: The mirrored injury feed lags the official page on game designations
flags.detail: For week 10 of 2026 the mirror holds 276 rows across 26 clubs with only 6 game designations, while the official page shows Out and Questionable for clubs inside 48 hours of kick-off.
flags.impact: Historical injury rules must be built on practice status, which is a weaker signal.

flags.item: Six clubs had no week-10 report at all
flags.detail: The mirror covers 26 of 32 clubs for week 10. A club with no rows is a club with no published report, not a healthy club. Zero is never written into a derived count for these clubs.
flags.impact: Any team-level availability index understates the clubs that did not report.

flags.item: 1,902 played games carry a closing line but no price
flags.detail: Every game before 2006, plus 28 games in 2026, has a spread or total with no price attached. Those games train the ratings and are never scored as bets.
flags.impact: The scoring sample is 5,228 games, not 7,103, and the difference is published rather than patched with an assumed -110.

flags.item: Same-game parlay prices are not published, so the size of the mispricing cannot be measured
flags.detail: The measured correlation between a quarterback's passing yards and his top receiver's receiving yards is +0.672. Books price same-game parlays in ways this repository cannot observe.
flags.impact: The site can say the product rule is wrong; it cannot say by how much in money.

flags.item: Historical depth charts are absent, so backup quality cannot be back-tested
flags.detail: Only the current season's depth charts were collected. Every historical injury rule therefore measures whether a starter is out, not how good the replacement is.
flags.impact: The single most requested feature of the brief is unvalidated.

flags.item: The incremental-information test and the raw edge correlation disagree
flags.detail: Regressing the result on both lines gives the model a weight of 0.161 with t = 3.35, while the raw correlation between the model's edge and the ATS result is 0.019 with p = 0.113.
flags.impact: Both are published. A reader who quotes only one will overstate the case in either direction.

flags.item: Five site generations now exist in one repository
flags.detail: Root, docs/, verified-lab/, referee/ and this section were built by different sessions and deliberately preserved rather than overwritten.
flags.impact: A reader cannot tell which numbers are current without reading COORDINATION.md.

flags.item: nfl.com prints Arizona as AZ while the feed uses ARI
flags.detail: The alias is applied for comparison only and is declared in the verification code. Without it, 9 of 136 game results and 1 of 32 standings rows appear to mismatch when the scores agree.
flags.impact: Any join between an nfl.com transcription and the feed needs the same alias.

flags.detail: An earlier session flagged that rewards with monetary value need legal review. The leaderboard here scores paper points only.

executive_summary.headline: We built our own lines over 7,239 games and scored 14,440 bets at real, observed prices. Our line is less accurate than the market's, but it still adds information the market does not have. No strategy survived all eight validation gates. That is the finding, and it is the useful one.

sections.title: What was built
items: A provenance-pinned research extract: 7,239 regular-season games 1999-2026, 24,932 skill-player weeks and 56,537 official injury rows, every source file pinned by URL and sha256.

Walk-forward own lines: ridge team ratings refitted for every (season, week) block using only games that finished earlier, with the recency half-life chosen on a validation slice of the training data.
A scored leaderboard: twelve rules, 14,440 bets, every bet priced from the source file, eight validation gates, Benjamini-Hochberg correction and an exact luck reference distribution.
A correlation register: eleven game-level and eight same-game player-prop correlations, every one with a Fisher-z 95% interval.
A parlay matrix: all 66 two-leg combinations priced at the product of their legs, with the realised dependence measured against independence.
Verification against official pages: 32/32 standings rows, 136/136 game results, 3/3 injury designations.

sections.title: The five findings that matter
items: The market line is more accurate than ours. Spread MAE 10.70 points against 10.24 over 6,975 games; the market line is closer to the result in a paired test with t = 10.33.

Our line still adds information. Regressing the result on both lines gives our line a weight of 0.161 with t = 3.35. The two facts are not in conflict: a line can be worse overall and still know something the better line does not.

Nothing passes. Zero of twelve strategies clear all eight gates. The closest, fading road favourites of seven or more, made 24.3 units where a lucky run would land inside plus or minus 19.0, and would need about 1,950 bets before that edge could be detected.

The strongest single result is a loss. Backing the under when the closing total is 40 or lower returned -7.93% over 887 bets (p = 0.015, BH-adjusted 0.178). It is either a real pricing bias or a sample artefact, and the honest response is to pre-register it and wait a season.

Parlay legs in different games really are independent. Across 66 combinations the realised joint hit rate divided by the product of the legs' own rates averages 1.0002. Inside one game they are emphatically not: a quarterback's passing yards and his top receiver's receiving yards correlate +0.672.

sections.title: What is unresolved
items: Player props have no price in any reachable official source, so no prop bet is scored and no prop profit is claimed. The track publishes projections, calibration and correlations only.
Historical depth charts are absent, so 'is the backup any good' cannot be back-tested. The current season has them; history does not.
The mirrored injury feed lags the official page on game designations by an unknown amount, which caps what any historical injury rule can use.
1,902 played games carry a line but no price. They train the ratings; they are never scored.

sections.title: What is being asked for
items: Decide whether to blend our line with the market line (suggestion S01) or publish ours raw.
Decide whether to fund historical depth charts (S02) or accept that backup quality stays unmeasured.
Decide whether the low-total finding is worth pre-registering for a season (S05).
Decide whether to consolidate the five site generations, which needs a cross-session request rather than a unilateral edit (S04).

executive_summary.not_advice: This is a research tool. Nothing on this site is betting advice, and no result here has been shown to beat the closing line after real prices.
